title: Genesis 26. The Cup Inherited.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 26. The Cup Inherited.
There was a famine in the land,
besides the first famine that was in the days of Abraham.
Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, to Gerar.
The same famine.
The same place.
The same king.
The man who was born to the promise walks into the same conditions his father walked into.
The Cup that was carried through Abraham's life now passes through the same terrain in Isaac's.
The Lord appeared to Isaac and said:
Do not go down to Egypt.
Dwell in the land I will tell you about.
Sojourn in this land,
and I will be with you and will bless you.
For to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands.
And I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.
I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands.
And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,
because Abraham obeyed My voice and kept My charge, My commandments,
My statutes, and My laws.
The covenant transfers.
The same words, stars, land, nations, blessing, spoken to the son.
But the reason given is not Isaac's faithfulness.
It is Abraham's.
Because Abraham obeyed.
The Cup that was given to the father is now held by the son for the father's sake.
The promise does not depend on the vessel.
It depends on the One who poured it,
and on the obedience of the man who first received it.
Isaac lived in Gerar.
And the men of the place asked him about his wife.
He said: She is my sister.
The same lie.
The third time in Genesis.
Abraham said it in Egypt.
Abraham said it in Gerar.
And now Isaac, the son who was born to the promise,
the son who was bound on Moriah,
the son who was comforted by Rebekah in Sarah's tent,
says it in the same city his father said it.
She is my sister.
The crack in the Cup is inherited.
The pattern does not merely repeat in one man,
it transfers across generations.
The son does what the father did.
The fear that made Abraham give Sarah to Pharaoh and Abimelech is the same fear that makes Isaac give Rebekah to the same Abimelech.
The vessel that fumbled in chapter twelve fumbles the same way in chapter twenty and fumbles again in chapter twenty-six.
The Cup holds.
The vessel does not change.
Isaac was afraid.
He thought: Lest the men of the place kill me for Rebekah,
because she is beautiful.
The woman who drew water for ten camels,
who said I will go, who entered Sarah's tent,
who was veiled before her husband,
is now given away by that same husband.
The Cup that was carried through a well and a journey and a veil is now endangered by the same fear that endangered it twice before.
When he had been there a long time,
Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out a window and saw Isaac caressing Rebekah his wife.
Abimelech called Isaac: Surely she is your wife.
Why did you say, She is my sister?
Isaac said: Because I thought, Lest I die because of her.
Abimelech said: What is this you have done to us?
One of the people might easily have lain with your wife,
and you would have brought guilt upon us!
For the third time, a pagan king rebukes the covenant holder.
Pharaoh rebuked Abraham.
Abimelech rebuked Abraham.
Now Abimelech rebukes Isaac.
The same king.
The same city.
The same lie.
The same exposure.
The Cup that was preserved in Abraham's time by God's intervention in a pagan king's dream is now preserved again,
by a pagan king looking out a window and seeing what the covenant holder was too afraid to say.
Abimelech commanded all the people:
Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.
The king who was deceived protects the deceiver.
The man who lied about his wife is now guarded by the king he lied to.
The Cup is preserved,
not by the vessel's faithfulness but by the integrity of the one who does not carry the covenant.
Then Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold.
The Lord blessed him.
The man became great and grew greater and greater until he became very great.
He had possessions of flocks and possessions of herds and a great household.
The Philistines envied him.
The Cup is inherited in fruitfulness.
The man who lied about his wife is blessed in the same land where he lied.
The vessel that fumbled is filled anyway.
The same God who preserved Sarah through Pharaoh and Abimelech,
who preserved Rebekah through the same Abimelech,
now multiplies Isaac a hundredfold in the land of the man he deceived.
The covenant does not depend on the vessel's perfection.
It depends on the One who fills it.
Now all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham,
the Philistines had stopped them and filled them with earth.
Abimelech said to Isaac: Go away from us,
for you are much mightier than we.
The wells are stopped.
What Abraham dug, the Philistines buried.
The Cup that was drawn from the ground in chapter twenty-one,
the well of Beersheba, the oath, the tamarisk tree,
is now filled with dirt.
The water that witnessed the covenant is covered by the people who envy the covenant's fruit.
Isaac departed from there and encamped in the valley of Gerar and lived there.
Isaac dug again the wells of water that they had dug in the days of Abraham his father,
which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham.
He called their names by the names his father had called them.
The Cup is inherited by re-digging what was buried.
Isaac does not dig new wells first.
He opens what his father opened.
He calls them what his father called them.
The promise does not begin fresh with each generation,
it recovers what was covered.
The vessel that inherits the Cup must first uncover what the previous vessel left in the ground.
But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying:
The water is ours.
He called the name of the well Esek, Contention,
because they contended with him.
They dug another well, and they quarreled over that also.
He called its name Sitnah, Enmity.
Esek.
Sitnah.
Contention.
Enmity.
The water that Abraham found is now contested by the people who buried it.
The Cup that was drawn in peace is now drawn in conflict.
The wells that were free when Abraham dug them are claimed by the Philistines who filled them.
The promise that was inherited must now be fought for,
not against enemies who never knew it,
but against neighbors who covered it.
He moved from there and dug another well,
and they did not quarrel over it.
He called its name Rehoboth, Room.
For he said: Now the Lord has made room for us,
and we shall be fruitful in the land.
Rehoboth.
Room.
The third well.
The place where the quarreling stops.
The Cup that was contested twice is finally held in peace,
not by winning the argument but by moving past it.
Isaac does not fight for Esek or Sitnah.
He digs again.
And the third well has no challenger.
The promise that was buried and uncovered and contested now finds room.
He went up from there to Beersheba.
The Lord appeared to him the same night and said:
I am the God of Abraham your father.
Do not fear, for I am with you.
I will bless you and multiply your offspring for My servant Abraham's sake.
Beersheba.
The place where Abraham planted a tamarisk tree and called on the name of the Lord,
the Everlasting God.
The place where the oath was sworn.
The place where the well was dug.
Isaac returns to it,
not by accident but by the same God who appeared to his father.
And the words are the same: Do not fear.
I am with you.
The Cup that was given to Abraham in fear and preserved in fear is now spoken over Isaac in the same words:
Do not fear.
He built an altar there and called on the name of the Lord and pitched his tent there.
And Isaac's servants dug a well there.
The same pattern.
God speaks.
Man builds an altar.
Servants dig a well.
The Cup is inherited in the same gestures, altar, tent, well.
Worship, dwelling, water.
What Abraham did at Shechem and Bethel and Hebron and Beersheba,
Isaac does at Beersheba.
The son walks in the father's footsteps.
Not perfectly.
Not cleanly.
But in the same direction.
Then Abimelech came to him from Gerar,
with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
Isaac said: Why have you come to me,
seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?
They said: We see plainly that the Lord is with you.
So we said, Let there be an oath between us,
between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm,
just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace.
You are now the blessed of the Lord.
The king who told Isaac to leave now comes back to make peace.
The man who was sent away is now sought out.
The same Abimelech who said Go away from us now says:
We see that the Lord is with you.
The Cup that was envied is now respected.
The vessel that was feared is now welcomed.
Not because Isaac changed.
Because the Cup he carried was seen.
He made them a feast, and they ate and drank.
They rose early in the morning and swore an oath to one another.
Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.
The same day,
Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug:
We have found water.
He called it Shibah.
Therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
Water again.
On the day the oath is made, the well is found.
The Cup that was buried and uncovered and contested and given room now flows again at Beersheba,
the same well Abraham's men dug,
the same place Abraham planted a tree,
the same city where God appeared as El Olam.
The water that witnessed the covenant in Abraham's generation now witnesses it in Isaac's.
When Esau was forty years old,
he took as wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite,
and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah.
The chapter ends with a crack.
The Cup has been inherited, the promise, the wells, the altar,
the oath, the water.
But the next generation is already breaking.
Esau, the hunter, the older,
the one who despised his birthright for a bowl of stew,
marries two Hittite women.
The same Hittites who sold Abraham a grave.
The same people of the land.
The covenant that was kept from Canaanite wives now faces Canaanite daughters in its own household.
The vessel that carries the Cup has a son who is marrying outside the line.
The Cup is inherited.
The same promise.
The same failure.
The same wells.
The same altar.
The same fear.
The same pagan king who rebukes and then seeks peace.
Isaac is walking in Abraham's footsteps, both the faith and the fear.
But God is with him.
Not because Isaac is perfect.
For Abraham's sake.
The covenant transfers through imperfection.
And the next generation's cracks are already showing.
The Cup holds.
The vessel does not.
